slides.title: Evaluating and Equivalent Expressions
slides.note: Post the learning target. Say the 'today' line and nothing else yet.

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.sub: On your own. Four minutes. No notes.
slides.note: Q4 is the prerequisite for the second half of today: one number, three bases. A board that stops at 8² has not yet seen that 8 is itself a power of 2 — that is Notes III.

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.note: Reveal. Ask for the band each question came from only if time allows.

slides.title: Notes
slides.note: Melanie applies the product law first (−2 + 5 = 3), then the quotient law. Adonis rewrites 5⁻² as 1/25 first and does arithmetic. Both reach 25. The teaching point from 3.03 again: apply the laws BEFORE evaluating when you can — the numbers stay small.

slides.title: Notes
slides.note: Power of a power (2 · −3 = −6), then quotient (−6 − (−5) = −1), then the negative exponent law to finish. Then the error-analysis pair from the book: the first student multiplied exponents where the product law adds; the second flipped a fraction without flipping the exponent. Both are on the board as 'find the step'.

slides.title: Notes
slides.note: 8 is 2³, so 8⁵ is (2³)⁵ = 2¹⁵. 9 is 3², so 9⁴ = 3⁸. And 2³ · 4³ = 2³ · (2²)³ = 2³ · 2⁶ = 2⁹. The table of squares, cubes and fourth powers from Unit 2 is the tool; the move is power of a power. Ask: which bases can be rewritten as powers of 2? (4, 8, 16, 32, 64.) Of 3? (9, 27, 81.)

slides.title: Notes
slides.note: Xavier says both expressions rewrite to 2⁻⁷. Rewrite each: (1/4)² = (2⁻²)² = 2⁻⁴, times 2⁻³ is 2⁻⁷. (1/2)⁴ = 2⁻⁴, times 4⁻¹ = 2⁻² is 2⁻⁶. Not equivalent — same base makes the comparison honest. This is the shape of whiteboard 9.

slides.title: Example 1
slides.note: SPOKEN ONLY. What does the negative exponent do to 3/4? Is the 3 outside part of the base? (No — it is a separate factor.)

slides.title: Example 1
slides.note: Flip, square, then multiply by 3. A student who writes (9/4)⁻² · 3 or (3/4)⁻⁶ pulled the 3 into the base. 16/3 is right; 5⅓ is the same value.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: Catches a student who folds the outside 2 into the base (board shows (4/5)⁻² or 4/25 · 2) and one who never flipped (4/25 · 2 = 8/25). 25/2 is right.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).

slides.title: Example 2
slides.note: SPOKEN ONLY. The two expressions have bases 3 and 6 on the left, and 3, 2 and 2 on the right. What base can 6 be broken into? Then both sides can be written with 3s and 2s only.

slides.title: Example 2
slides.note: Left: 6³ = (3·2)³ = 3³·2³, so 3⁵·2³. Right: (3·2)⁵ = 3⁵·2⁵, over 2² leaves 3⁵·2³. Identical, so equivalent; the value is 243 · 8 = 1944 if anyone wants it.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: Catches a student who cannot split 10 into 2 · 5 (board stops at 10³) and one who subtracts the wrong exponent on the right. Both are 2⁵ · 5³; yes.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).
